title: Remote work trends employers should watch.
summary: Remote work is holding steady even as mandates spread. See the remote work trends shaping policy, retention, and early-career development for employers.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


- Remote work has held steady at about a quarter of paid workdays, so employers should plan around today's mix of remote, hybrid, and on-site work.
- Return-to-office mandates raise attendance less than policies require and carry ongoing enforcement costs.
- Employers are trimming standing flexibility in favor of temporary options, which makes clear remote terms in job postings a recruiting advantage.
- Hybrid schedules help retain employees, while strict mandates increase turnover among senior and highly skilled talent.
- Early-career employees lose the most from distance, so employers need a deliberate plan for mentoring and feedback, whether teams meet in person or work remotely.


The years that have passed since the pandemic pushed remote work into the spotlight have made expectations around policies harder to read. Remote work is no longer the default it seemed to be in 2021, yet many top candidates are still looking for it. For employers with roles that can be done remotely, deciding whether to offer it, and how much, is rarely clear-cut. The wrong call can cost you candidates, experienced employees, and the next generation of talent.


Return-to-office mandates keep getting stricter, but the share of work done from home has held steady. The remote work trends below show what those steady numbers mean for recruiting, retention, and development. Across all of them, employers come out ahead when they design each work arrangement deliberately, using in-office time where it helps most and building structure into remote work. That planning matters most for early-career employees, who tend to pay the highest price for distance.


## Remote work by the numbers


Government data, academic research, and workplace surveys each measure remote work differently, but all of them point to a stable share of the workweek.


- [26% of paid workdays](https://wfhresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/WFHResearch_updates_September2026.pdf) in the U.S. were remote in July 2026.


- Among full-time employees,


[12% are fully remote, 26% are hybrid, and 62% are fully on site](https://wfhresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/WFHResearch_updates_September2026.pdf) .


- [52% of remote-capable employees](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/713093/hybrid-work-productivity.aspx) work a hybrid schedule.


- [35% of employed people](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/atus_06252026.htm) did some or all of their work at home on days they worked in 2025.


- [27% of employers](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-research-reveals-the-strategic-benefits-shifts-reshaping-th) now offer limited-time work-from-anywhere arrangements.


The figures differ because each survey counts something different, from full days worked at home to any work done at home on a given day. For planning, use full-day figures to estimate office space needs and part-day figures to schedule meetings and team time.

## Remote work has found its level


Years into the return-to-office push, the share of work done from home has barely moved.


[Between 21.5% and 23% of U.S. workers teleworked](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/22-6-percent-of-workers-teleworked-in-march-2026.htm) in each month of the year ending March 2026, and employer plans have settled at about the same level. Remote work is now a fixed feature of the labor market, so the open question for employers is how to design around it. Plan headcount, office space, and policy on the assumption that today's mix of remote, hybrid, and on-site work will hold.


The share of U.S. job ads offering at least one remote day per week


[more than tripled from 2019 to 2026](https://www.dallasfed.org/research/papers/2026/wp2629) . The more telling finding is how much employers differ. Companies in the same industry, recruiting for the same occupations, make very different offers. When competitors offer different terms for the same role, a remote policy becomes part of the offer, whether or not it was designed that way.


The right amount of remote work also depends on the role. In June 2026,


[52.5% of workers in financial activities teleworked, compared with 7.7% in leisure and hospitality](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/52-5-percent-of-workers-in-financial-activities-teleworked-in-june-2026.htm) . A single companywide policy rarely fits a workforce that spans finance, operations, and frontline roles. Setting expectations by role family, based on how the work gets done, gives managers a policy they can defend to candidates and employees alike.


## Mandates are rising faster than attendance


Executives expect a full return to the office, but employees covered by mandates come in less often than their policies require.


**Executive intent is clear.** In 2024,


[83% of CEOs worldwide expected a full return to the office within three years](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/media/press-releases/2024/09/top-ceos-navigate-global-turbulence-by-betting-big-on-ai.html) . That window closes in 2027, and work-from-home levels have yet to move toward it. Leaders who plan around that expectation risk building space, schedules, and performance systems for a workforce that may never arrive in full.


**Attendance trails policy.** Badge data from a Fortune 500 retailer shows how far practice can drift from policy. After the company required engineers in the office three days a week,


[average attendance rose to 1.9 days](https://pallais.scholars.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum5926/files/2026-05/Power_of_Proximity_2026_1.pdf) . A mandate moves attendance, but not necessarily to the number written in the policy. Employers who plan desk space and collaboration days around the official requirement will overestimate who shows up.


**Enforcement has a price.** When the IRS ended routine telework in 2025,


[the share of employees using any telework fell from 65% to 25%](https://www.tigta.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-03/2026ier004fr.pdf) . Verifying compliance took ongoing effort. About 11% of in-person time records had no matching badge data, and resolving those records required manual review by managers and business units. Every mandate carries an administrative cost in tracking, reconciling records, and managing exceptions. Employers weighing a stricter policy should budget for that cost and ask whether the in-office time it buys goes to the work that benefits most from people being together.


## Flexibility is getting narrower and harder to read


Employers are trading broad, standing flexibility for narrower and more temporary options, and candidates often can't tell which kind a job includes until after they accept the offer.


- Standing flexibility is shrinking. Between SHRM's 2025 and 2026 benefits surveys, the


[share of employers offering core-hours flextime fell 6 points](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-research-reveals-the-strategic-benefits-shifts-reshaping-th) , and the share offering hybrid work fell 3 points.


- Temporary options are growing.


[Twenty-seven percent of employers](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-research-reveals-the-strategic-benefits-shifts-reshaping-th) now offer limited-time work-from-anywhere arrangements.


- Advertised terms don't always match the job. In a Kelly survey,


[54% of hiring managers admitted to misrepresenting remote work availability to secure hires](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/dishonest-job-search-survey-results) , and 76% of job seekers reported discrepancies in remote work expectations.


Temporary flexibility can be a smart, low-cost benefit, but unclear terms create risk. When flexibility shows up as exceptions and short-term arrangements, candidates have a harder time knowing what a role offers, and mismatched expectations surface after the hire, when they cost more to fix.


Clear remote terms also become a competitive advantage while flexibility is scarce. Spell out in job postings and offers which days are in the office, which arrangements are temporary, and who approves exceptions. For roles that are remote by design,


[setting expectations early in the hiring process](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/remote-staffing-agency) sets candidates up for success. At Kelly, recruiters work with clients to revise job descriptions before a remote role goes live, so the posting reflects the skills, schedule, and day-to-day work the role requires. Feedback from new hires then shapes the description for the next round.


## Flexibility has become a retention lever


The most rigorous research on remote work links hybrid schedules to lower turnover. In a


[randomized trial of 1,612 employees](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07500-2) , a two-day-per-week hybrid schedule cut quit rates by one-third, with no effect on performance reviews over two years. Quit rates among women in the hybrid group fell by 54%. For employers, those results make hybrid work a retention tool with a measurable payoff.


Research on mandates points the other way. After S&P 500 tech and financial firms announced return-to-office mandates,


[average employee turnover rose 14%](https://ssrn.com/abstract=5031481) , with larger increases among senior, highly skilled, and female employees. Senior and highly skilled employees are often the hardest to replace, so a strict mandate can cost an employer the experience they hoped to bring back into the office.


Most employees aren't asking for fully remote roles. Only


[24% of hybrid workers](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/01/13/many-remote-workers-say-theyd-be-likely-to-leave-their-job-if-they-could-no-longer-work-from-home/) say they would work from home all the time if they could choose. A predictable hybrid schedule, set in advance and paired with


[activities that keep hybrid teams connected](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/employee-engagement-activities) , meets what most of these employees want and carries less risk than either extreme.


Support after the hire matters too. Kelly recruiters stay the point of contact for remote employees after placement and hold performance conversations throughout the year. Kelly has supported


[one pharmaceutical client's team of 29 fully remote employees](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/remote-staffing-agency) this way for several years.


## Early-career development is the overlooked tradeoff


The cost of distance falls hardest on employees who are still learning their jobs, and the impact rarely shows up in productivity or retention reports, so it’s easy to miss.


### Distance hits junior employees hardest


New research suggests remote work has made it harder for young professionals to get a foothold. Economists behind a


[2026 study of proximity and feedback](https://pallais.scholars.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum5926/files/2026-05/Power_of_Proximity_2026_1.pdf) estimate that remote work accounts for 64% of the rise in unemployment among young college graduates between 2017 to 2019 and 2022 to 2024. The same study found that sitting near teammates increased the feedback software engineers received on their code by 18.3%, with the biggest gains for younger and less-tenured employees.


Feedback on everyday work is how junior employees build judgment. In an office, much of it happens in passing, during a quick question at a desk or a review that turns into a conversation. Distributed teams lose many of those moments, and early-career employees feel the loss most.


### Employers are already hiring around it


When offices close, some employers change who they hire. At the company in the proximity study, more than half of new engineers were under 29 before offices closed and after they reopened, but fewer than a third were under 29 during the closure. Hiring experienced people can feel like the safe choice when no one is around to train newcomers.


But that choice creates a future problem. In a Kelly survey of global executives,


[56% said recent graduates lack workplace professionalism](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/top-hiring-challenges-2026) , and 43% said they struggle to apply concepts in practice. The same executives see promise, with


[62% describing recent graduates as innovative and resourceful](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/future-of-work-trends-2025-kelly-rework-report-insights) . Early-career talent has potential that needs development. Skipping entry-level hiring leaves that potential untapped and thins the bench employers will need as experienced workers retire.


### Build development into every work arrangement


Early-career development holds up in any work model when employers plan deliberately for how junior employees learn. For hybrid teams, who comes in together matters as much as how many days people come in. In the proximity study, having just one teammate in another building


[reduced feedback among the rest of the team by 14.5%](https://pallais.scholars.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum5926/files/2026-05/Power_of_Proximity_2026_1.pdf) . An office day delivers the most value when the people a junior employee learns from are there too.


Fully or mostly remote teams need structure to replace what proximity provides on its own. A few practices help:


- Schedule feedback. Regular work reviews and short one-on-ones recreate the coaching that happens in passing in an office.


- Assign mentors. Pairing each new hire with an experienced colleague gives them a go-to person for questions they might not raise in a group channel.


- Make work visible. Recorded walkthroughs, shared documents, and open project channels help junior employees learn by seeing how experienced colleagues work.


- Meet in person occasionally. Periodic team gatherings build the relationships that make remote feedback easier to give and receive.


Clear


[learning paths for new employees](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/how-to-upskill-your-employees) support early-career talent in every model, and so does career visibility. Kelly gives every remote hire a clear career timeline up front, covering where they are now and what the next 12 to 18 months look like, because remote employees who can't see a path forward are more likely to disengage. These investments make entry-level hiring less risky, which keeps the pipeline of future experienced workers open.


## Plan for every work model with Kelly


Remote work has settled into a stable share of the workweek, so the advantage goes to employers who decide how each kind of work gets done best and plan around it. For hybrid teams, coordinate in-office days by team, so the people who learn from each other are in the same place. For remote teams, build feedback, mentoring, and visible work into the regular workweek. In every model, protect development time for early-career employees and state remote terms plainly in every job posting and offer.
